extracted.intended_audience: aviation professionals, accident investigators, regulators, journalists, and general readers interested in the Lion Air 737 MAX accident and its regulatory/operator implications
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, findings, and regulatory actions relevant to investigating and reporting an aircraft accident (Lion Air Flight 610), including design/ certification issues, flight manuals, operator communications, pilot training, and repair-station oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid single-point-of-failure designs
rubrics_metrics.description: A nose-down command triggered by a sensor single point of failure is a design flaw if the crew is not prepared
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NTSC/following investigations considered a single AoA sensor triggering a nose-down command (MCAS) a design flaw when the crew lacked preparation; investigators evaluated fixes and whether pilots' transition training was adequate. The malfunction of the captain-side AoA sensor caused MCAS to continuously trim nose-down, contributing to the crash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flight manual must include operating limitations/procedures for erroneous AoA data
rubrics_metrics.description: An emergency airworthiness directive required that amended operating limitations and procedures relating to erroneous data from an AoA sensor be inserted into the aircraft flight manual of each 737 MAX aircraft
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. FAA issued this AD (7 November) on the basis of preliminary information from the Lion Air investigation and urged all airlines operating 737 MAX 8s to heed the warnings. The AD effectively mandates specific documentation and procedures in operator manuals to address erroneous AoA sensor data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repair-station certification and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Repair stations that fix components (e.g., AoA sensors) must meet certification standards; certification can be revoked if repairs are implicated in accidents
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On 25 October 2019 the FAA revoked the repair certification of Xtra Aerospace LLC after an AoA sensor they fixed was suspected of contributing to the crash; revocation can effectively put a repair firm out of business. This underscores regulatory oversight and quality-control expectations for repair stations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference training must disclose all significant system differences (e.g., MCAS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilots converting from earlier Boeing 737 Next Generation models to the 737 MAX were not informed of the MCAS linked to the fatal crash
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aviation Week's review found the 737 MAX flight-crew operations manual did not mention MCAS; pilot groups (American, Southwest) reported being unaware. The absence of system disclosure in difference training was a central concern and is treated as a training deficiency by unions and investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flight-crew operations manuals should describe relevant automatic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers/operators should ensure the flight-crew operations manual describes relevant automatic system functions (for example, MCAS)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boeing defended its manual as describing MCAS, while independent reviews found omissions. The dispute highlights the expectation that manuals clearly document automatic systems and their effects so flight crews understand behavior and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturers should brief operators and allow questions about new systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers should disclose new automatic systems to operators and provide forums for questions (e.g., conference calls to detail MCAS)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boeing planned a global conference call with 737 MAX operators to detail MCAS; it was later replaced by regional calls to allow more questions. This demonstrates an expectation for proactive manufacturer-operator communication and technical briefing when introducing system changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilots must have clear, standard procedures to disable/shut down malfunctioning flight-control behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilot guidance/manuals should include standard procedures to shut down problematic flight-control behavior
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some carriers/management contended the 737 pilot manual included a standard procedure to shut down the flight-control behavior (used to downplay MCAS implication). Regardless of debate, the presence, clarity, and training on such procedures are treated as essential to safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulators/investigators must ensure pilots receive all relevant information about potential significant safety deficiencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory bodies should ensure information flow to pilots addressing any 'potential, significant aviation system safety deficiency.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Air Line Pilots Association urged the FAA and NTSB to ensure pilots receive relevant information. This captures an oversight expectation that authorities verify both disclosure and the adequacy of training/information relating to system safety concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design, certification, and oversight must prevent recurrence of unsafe flight-control conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions should be taken to address safety recommendations and enhance safety to prevent the flight-control conditions that occurred from happening again
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following the NTSC final report, Boeing stated it was addressing safety recommendations to prevent recurrence. The broader rubric implied by the investigation: robust design review, rigorous certification, and effective oversight are required to avoid systemic failures leading to accidents.
